passages.t: After the birth of a son or a daughter
passages.happening:
The LORD tells Moses what to say to Israel. “A woman who becomes pregnant and gives birth to a son will be unclean for seven days, as she is during the days of her menstruation” (verse 2). “And on the eighth day the flesh of the boy’s foreskin is to be circumcised” (verse 3).

“The woman shall continue in purification from her bleeding for thirty-three days. She must not touch anything sacred or go into the sanctuary until the days of her purification are complete” (verse 4).

“If, however, she gives birth to a daughter, the woman will be unclean for two weeks as she is during her menstruation. Then she must continue in purification from her bleeding for sixty-six days” (verse 5).
passages.hearers:
This is the first of the laws about the human body, and it begins where human life begins.

A new reader must be clear about one thing before anything else. Unclean does not mean sinful. The Bible never treats the birth of a child as shameful. Children are God's first blessing on humanity: “Be fruitful and multiply” (Genesis 1:28). A psalm calls them ‘a heritage from the LORD’ (Psalm 127:3). Nothing in this chapter says the mother has done wrong.

What does unclean mean, then? It means that for a time she does not go to the sanctuary or handle holy things. Many scholars, following Jacob Milgrom, see one thread running through chapters 11 to 15. Uncleanness gathers round the loss of the fluids that carry life, and round the nearness of death. These were kept back from the house of the living God. Childbirth brings new life into the world. It also involves the loss of blood, and in the ancient world it was among the most dangerous hours of a woman's life. Rachel died giving birth to Benjamin (Genesis 35:17-18). So birth stands right on the line between life and death, and the law marks it.

The time comes in two stages. For the first seven days after a son, or fourteen after a daughter, the mother's state is like that of her monthly period. In the longer second stage, as most interpreters understand it, she no longer passes uncleanness to others. She simply stays away from holy things. The text calls these ‘the days of her purification’. The word looks forward to being clean again.

The forty days after a son roughly match the weeks of bleeding that follow a birth. They also gave a new mother a long time free from the demands of public worship. Many traditional cultures still keep a rest of about forty days after a birth.

Verse 3 mentions, in passing, the sign of God's covenant with Abraham. Every boy in Israel received it on the eighth day of his life.
passages.later:
God gave the sign to Abraham: “every male must be circumcised when he is eight days old” (Genesis 17:12).

Luke tells how this law was kept for Jesus. “When the eight days until His circumcision had passed, He was named Jesus” (Luke 2:21). Then, “when the time of purification according to the Law of Moses was complete, His parents brought Him to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord” (Luke 2:22).

Paul sums it up: “God sent His Son, born of a woman, born under the law” (Galatians 4:4). The Son of God came into the world through the bodily process this chapter is about, and his mother kept its days.
passages.hard:
Why does giving birth make a woman unclean? And why for twice as long after a daughter?

Two misunderstandings need clearing away first. Uncleanness in Leviticus is not sin. And it is not shame. The chapter does not say that a woman's body is dirty, that birth is a disgrace, or that a mother is under God's displeasure. A husband and wife were unclean until evening after they slept together (15:18). A person who buried a parent was unclean for a week (Numbers 19:11). No one had done wrong in either case. The mother's uncleanness is of the same kind: a state that passes with time, and that keeps the loss of blood away from the sanctuary.

The doubled time after a daughter has no stated reason, and interpreters differ. Some see in it the lower standing of women in the ancient world. Others suggest that the baby girl will one day be a mother herself, so that her birth is doubly linked with blood and life; some add that newborn girls sometimes bleed slightly in their first days. Others link the shorter time after a son to his circumcision on the eighth day, which begins a new stage. These notes do not choose among them.

Whatever the reason, the chapter does not value a daughter less where it matters most. The offering for her birth is exactly the same as the offering for a son, and verse 7 names both.

The church remembered this law in its own way. Many churches kept a service of thanksgiving for a mother after childbirth. It was shaped more by gratitude for a safe delivery than by any idea of uncleanness.

No one may use this chapter to tell a woman that her body, her bleeding or her giving birth makes her less in God's sight. A word for anyone who has been made to feel unclean, by an illness, by your body or by your past. That is not what this book says of you. Your worth to God does not rise or fall with your body. If the weight of it is heavy, please share it with someone you trust: a friend, a pastor, a doctor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The law gave a new mother weeks in which nothing was asked of her at the sanctuary. Ask who near you has just had a child, and what would truly give her rest. And ask whether you have ever let someone feel that their body, or what it has been through, puts them further from God.

passages.happening:
“When the days of her purification are complete, whether for a son or for a daughter, she is to bring to the priest at the entrance to the Tent of Meeting a year-old lamb for a burnt offering and a young pigeon or a turtledove for a sin offering” (verse 6).

The priest presents them and makes atonement for her, and she is clean. “This is the law for a woman giving birth, whether to a male or to a female” (verse 7).

“But if she cannot afford a lamb, she shall bring two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for a burnt offering and the other for a sin offering. Then the priest will make atonement for her, and she will be clean” (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The offerings mark the mother's return to the full worship of Israel. She comes herself, to the entrance of the tent, with her own offering in her hands.

The burnt offering is the whole gift of chapter 1, an act of giving oneself to God. The second is called a ‘sin offering’, and the name can mislead. The same Hebrew word means purification, and many scholars call it the purification offering. It is brought here where no sin is in view. It cleanses the effects of her time of uncleanness and brings her back to the sanctuary. ‘Atonement’ in Leviticus covers more than the forgiveness of wrongs. It also covers the uncleanness that comes simply from living in a body that bleeds and dies.

The last line of the passage is not about guilt. It says, ‘she will be clean’.

Notice two things. The offering is the same for a son and for a daughter. Each child is received as a gift. And verse 8 repeats the mercy of chapter 5. A poor mother brings two birds. No family is shut out of thanking God for a child because it cannot afford a lamb.
passages.later:
Mary brought the offering of verse 8. Luke says that she and Joseph came “to offer the sacrifice specified in the Law of the Lord: ‘A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons’” (Luke 2:24). It tells the reader, without comment, that Jesus was born into a household that could not afford a lamb.

Hannah, too, came to the house of the LORD with her child and her offering, when Samuel was weaned (1 Samuel 1:24).
passages.asks: The poorest mother in Israel could bring her thanks for a child, and hear that she was clean. Ask how your church receives a new child, and whether a poor family is welcomed there as warmly as a rich one. And ask what gift of God you have received and not yet thanked him for.
